title: Start With Your Own Problem
subtitle: Bring a real situation — a decision, a stuck team, an impossible week — and leave with a tool, the language to use it, and a plan you have said out loud.
intro: Every tool in this collection was invented because somebody had a problem they could not hold in their head. Today the problem is yours.
Work through the three steps. You do the talking; the page just keeps the questions coming.

step1.heading: Step 1 · Say the situation out loud
step1.lead: Before you choose a tool, describe what is actually happening. Take two minutes and answer these.
prompts: What is the situation, in one sentence? Say it as a fact, not as a complaint.
Who else is involved, and what do they want?
How will you know when it is better? What exactly will be different?
step1.note: If your sentence contains a person's name and the word “always”, try again. Describe what happens, not who is to blame.

step2.heading: Step 2 · Choose your tool
step2.lead: Read the descriptions and click the one that sounds most like your situation. You will get the tool, the questions it asks, and the language you need.

step3.heading: Step 3 · Use it, out loud
step3.lead: Now run the tool on your own situation, speaking the whole way through. Use the timer if you want a target.
frame: Sort it: talk through the tool's questions, one at a time, putting your own details into each box, stage or level.
Argue with yourself: “Somebody might say … , but I'd answer …”
Decide: “So the first thing I'm going to do is … , by … .”
final: Which part of the tool was hardest to answer honestly? Why?
What did the tool miss about your situation?
Would the people involved agree with the way you filled it in?
If nothing changes for six months, what will you do then?

tools.when: Too much to do, never enough time
asks: How urgent is it?
How important is it?
steps: Write down everything on your mind — work, home, people, promises.
Ask the importance question first, then the urgency question.
Put each one in a box: do now, schedule, delegate, drop.
Give the “important, not urgent” box a real day and time in your calendar.
phrases: It feels urgent, but it isn't important.
I have to … , but I don't have to …
I need to make time for …

tools.when: Many problems, and I can only fix one or two
asks: Which few causes produce most of the trouble?
What does the evidence say, not the loudest voice?
steps: Count something real: complaints, faults, hours, money, interruptions.
Put the causes in order, biggest first.
Add them up until you reach about 80% — those are your vital few.
Fix them first, then count again.
phrases: Most of the problem comes from …
That's a small minority, so it can wait.

tools.when: The same thing keeps going wrong
tools.tool: The Fishbone Diagram and the Five Whys
asks: What are all the possible causes?
And why did each of those happen?
steps: Write the problem as a fact at the head of the fish — never as a person.
Fill the big bones: people, methods, machines, materials, measurement, environment.
Choose the most likely bone and ask “why?” about five times, until you reach a system you can change.
Fix that, then watch whether the problem comes back.
phrases: The real root cause might be …

tools.when: Something might go wrong and I don't know how much to worry
asks: How likely is it?
How serious would it be?
steps: List what could go wrong, plainly, and to whom.
Score each one for likelihood — using what has actually happened before.
Score each one for consequence — the realistic worst case.
Act on the red corner, and on anything that could hurt somebody, whatever its score.
phrases: It's unlikely — however, if it happened, …

tools.when: A team, class or family group that isn't working
asks: Which stage is this group in?
What does that stage need?
steps: Name the stage out loud: forming, storming, norming, performing or ending.
If it is polite and slow, bring the real disagreement into the open.
If it is stormy, argue about the work and not the person — then agree how you will operate.
Write down what you agreed, and protect it when somebody new arrives.

tools.when: A decision about somebody's future at work
asks: How well are they performing now?
How far could they grow?
steps: Decide what performance means in this job — using evidence, not feelings.
Decide what potential would look like, and what would prove it.
Place the person, then argue the placement with somebody who sees them differently.
Agree one action: a bigger project, support, honest feedback — and a date to look again.
phrases: Her results are far stronger than …
The more responsibility she gets, the more …

tools.when: I don't know how other people see me
asks: What do I know about myself?
What do other people know?
steps: Write six words that describe you. Ask two people you trust to write six about you.
Words you both chose are open. Words only they chose are your blind spot.
Choose one thing to tell people, to make the hidden part smaller.
Ask one specific question for feedback — “what do I do in meetings that annoys you?” beats “any feedback?”
phrases: People often think I seem … , but actually …

tools.when: Two sides could work together — but neither will move first
asks: What does each side get for cooperating or not?
Will we meet again?
steps: Draw the grid: their two choices across, yours down, and what each of you gets in every box.
Ask whether the best box for both of you is different from the safest box for you alone.
If you will meet again, use the winning strategy: be nice first, answer betrayal once, forgive quickly, be predictable.
Look for something that changes the payoffs: a rule, a contract, a witness, a habit.

tools.when: A big decision about my work, my studies or an organisation
asks: What is inside my control — strengths and weaknesses?
What is outside it — opportunities and threats?
steps: Write the goal first. A strength for one goal is a weakness for another.
Fill the internal boxes honestly, including the weaknesses you would rather not write.
Fill the external boxes: what is changing around you?
Then ask “so what?” — pair each strength with an opportunity or a threat, and choose two actions.
phrases: One of my biggest strengths is …
An external threat I can't control is …

tools.when: Something is wrong and I can't say what
asks: Which needs are met?
Which is the lowest one with a real gap?
steps: Go up the levels for yourself or the person you're thinking of: body, safety, belonging, respect, growth.
Be honest about the lowest level with a gap — sleep and money are not embarrassing answers.
Do one concrete thing for that level this week.
Remember the levels overlap: friendship helps even when the bottom is shaky.

tools.when: I need other people to accept something new
asks: Who adopts new things early here?
What would the cautious majority need to see?
steps: Find the innovators — they'll try it because it is new.
Win the early adopters: the people others watch. Give them something to show.
For the majority, supply proof and stories from people like them, and make it simple.
For the last group, remove the obstacles — or accept that some never will.
phrases: Once a few colleagues had tried it, …

tools.when: I'm living between two countries or cultures
asks: Am I keeping my own culture?
Am I taking part in the wider society?
steps: Answer the two questions separately — and notice that the answers differ at work and at home.
Ask what has changed since your first year here.
Ask the second half of the question: what does this place allow or block?
Choose one practical step towards “yes and yes”: a club, a class, a conversation, a tradition kept alive.
phrases: In my first year I was probably …
At work I … , but at home I …
The place where I feel most myself is …

tools.when: Everything is changing faster than I can react
asks: What is actually happening now?
Which of my assumptions is out of date?
steps: Observe: gather what has changed, not what you expected.
Orient: this is the step that matters. Name the assumption you may be wrong about.
Decide one action — not five.
Act, then go straight back to observing: what has changed because of what you did?
phrases: As soon as I noticed … , I …
Once I'd understood … , I decided to …
